body.en: ACT Math 2 is an advanced subject-level mathematics course for students who have completed standard ACT Math preparation and wish to extend their skills into pre-calculus territory — the topics that appear in the hardest ACT questions and on ACT subject tests.

label.en: ● Deep Conceptual Intuition — Test format & strategy

body.en: Proportional Invariance, Linear Structure & Quantitative Modeling: Across ACT International Subject Test — Math 1, multi-step problems reduce to identifying invariant quantities—constant rates of change \(m = \dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\), conservation of total work/mass, or linear system rank conditions. A two-variable linear system \(a_1 x + b_1 y = c_1\), \(a_2 x + b_2 y = c_2\) has a unique intersection if \(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} \ne \dfrac{b_1}{b_2}\), no solution (parallel lines) if \(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_1}{b_2} \ne \dfrac{c_1}{c_2}\), and infinitely many solutions if all three ratios coincide.

body.en: This course covers the top-difficulty ACT Math topics: advanced algebra, pre-calculus functions, matrices, advanced trigonometry, and non-routine geometry. It is also ideal preparation for the ACT Subject Test in Mathematics, which tests material through pre-calculus.

label.en: ⏱ ACT Subject Math 1 Pacing & Time Management Strategy

body.en:
• Pacing Baseline: 50 questions in 60 minutes = 72 seconds per question. There is no guessing penalty — every unanswered question is a lost opportunity.
  • Three-Pass Strategy: Pass 1 (Questions 1–25, ~20 min): bank easy points rapidly. Pass 2 (Questions 26–45, ~25 min): methodical solving of mid-level algebra, trig, and coordinate geometry. Pass 3 (Questions 46–50 & review, ~15 min): tackle non-routine multi-step items and ensure all bubble answers are filled.
  • Approved Calculator Fluency: Graphing calculators are permitted throughout. Store formulas, use matrix inverse/determinant functions, and verify complex number arithmetic \(a + bi\) directly.

label.en: ▲ The 4 Core Commandments for Scoring 30+ on ACT Advanced Math

body.en:
• 1. Never Leave Blanks: Unlike old SAT Subject tests, there is zero penalty for incorrect answers. If time is running short with 2 minutes remaining, pick a favorite letter (e.g., C or D) and fill every remaining bubble.
  • 2. Identify Conic Signatures at a Glance: In \(Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0\), same signs on \(x^2\) and \(y^2\) with \(A = C\) indicates a circle; same signs with \(A \neq C\) indicates an ellipse; opposite signs indicates a hyperbola; only one squared term indicates a parabola.
  • 3. Exploit Backsolving & Number Substitution: When an algebraic equation has complex fractions, logs, or radicals, testing answer choice C (the median value) first often eliminates 2–3 options in under 30 seconds.
  • 4. Memorize the Critical Edge-Case Formulas: Circle inscribed angle \(=\frac{1}{2}\text{central}\), Heron's formula \(A = \sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}\), sum of infinite geometric series \(S_\infty = \frac{a}{1-r}\), and vector dot product \(\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v} = u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2\).

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Test format & strategy)

body.en:
Why Successive Multipliers & Harmonic Average Speed Work: If a quantity \(Q_0\) undergoes a percentage change \(p\%\) followed by \(q\%\), the compound multiplier is the product of individual scale factors:

\[ Q_{\text{final}} = Q_0\left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right)\!\left(1 + \frac{q}{100}\right) = Q_0\left(1 + \frac{p + q}{100} + \frac{pq}{10000}\right) \]

Notice the cross term \(\dfrac{pq}{10000}\): an increase of \(p\%\) followed by a decrease of \(p\%\) yields \(Q_0\bigl(1 - (p/100)^2\bigr) < Q_0\). Similarly, traveling equal distance \(d\) at speeds \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) takes total time \(T = \frac{d}{v_1} + \frac{d}{v_2}\), so average speed is the harmonic mean \(v_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{2d}{d/v_1 + d/v_2} = \dfrac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}\).

label.en: Worked Example A — Test format & strategy (Easy Application)

body.en:
Problem (Easy): What is the smallest positive integer \( n \) such that \( 126n \) is the square of an integer?

Step-by-Step Solution: To find the smallest positive integer \( n \) such that \( 126n \) is a perfect square, first find the prime factorization of 126: \[ 126 = 2 \times 63 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 7 \] For an integer to be a perfect square, every prime factor in its prime factorization must have an even exponent. In the prime factorization of 126: - The factor 2 has an exponent of 1 (odd). - The factor 3 has an exponent of 2 (even). - The factor 7 has an exponent of 1 (odd). To make all exponents even with the smallest positive integer \( n \), \( n \) must provide at least one factor of 2 and one factor of 7: \[ n = 2^1 \times 7^1 = 14 \] Then \( 126 \times 14 = 1764 = 42^2 \), which is a perfect square. Common misconceptions: - Choosing 7 only pairs the factor 7, leaving 2 with an odd exponent (\( 126 \times 7 = 882 \), not a square). - Choosing 21 multiplies by \( 3 \times 7 \), leaving 2 unpaired. - Choosing 42 gives \( 126 \times 42 = 5292 \), which is not a square and is greater than 14. Final Answer: \( 14 \).

label.en: Worked Example \(B\) — Test format & strategy (Easy Application)

body.en:
Problem (Easy): In right triangle \(ABC\), altitude \(\overline{BD}\) is drawn to hypotenuse \(\overline{AC}\). If \(AD = 4\) and \(DC = 9\), what is the length of altitude \(\overline{BD}\)?

Step-by-Step Solution: By the Geometric Mean Theorem (Altitude Rule) for right triangles, the altitude to the hypotenuse is the geometric mean of the two segments into which it divides the hypotenuse: \[ BD^2 = AD \cdot DC \] Substitute the given lengths \(AD = 4\) and \(DC = 9\): \[ BD^2 = 4 \cdot 9 = 36 \] Taking the positive square root: \[ BD = \sqrt{36} = 6 \] Common Misconceptions: - Choice B (6.5) confuses the geometric mean with the arithmetic mean: \(\frac{4 + 9}{2} = 6.5\). - Choice C (13) incorrectly adds the two segments together: \(4 + 9 = 13\). - Choice D (36) finds \(BD^2 = 4 \times 9\) but forgets to take the square root.

label.en: Worked Example \(C\) — Test format & strategy (Easy Application)

body.en:
Problem (Easy): What is the period of the function \( f(x) = 3\cos(2x) \)?

Step-by-Step Solution: The standard form of a cosine function is \( f(x) = A\cos(Bx) \), where the amplitude is \( |A| \) and the period is \( \dfrac{2\pi}{|B|} \). For the function \( f(x) = 3\cos(2x) \), the coefficient of \( x \) is \( B = 2 \). Applying the period formula: \[ \text{Period} = \dfrac{2\pi}{2} = \pi \] Common misconceptions: - Choice A (\( \frac{\pi}{2} \)) comes from incorrectly dividing \( \pi \) by \( B \) (the formula for the period of tangent). - Choice C (\( 2\pi \)) forgets to account for the horizontal compression factor \( B = 2 \). - Choice D (\( 4\pi \)) mistakenly multiplies \( 2\pi \) by \( 2 \) rather than dividing.

label.en: Worked Example \(D\) — Test format & strategy (Easy Application)

body.en:
Problem (Easy): The bar graph below shows the number of students enrolled in each of four elective courses at a high school. If one student is selected at random from these four courses, what is the probability that the selected student is enrolled in Music?

Step-by-Step Solution: To find the probability that a randomly chosen student is enrolled in Music, divide the number of students enrolled in Music by the total number of students enrolled across all four courses. 1. Find the total number of students: \[ \text{Total} = 8 + 14 + 6 + 12 = 40 \] 2. Find the number of students in Music: \[ n(\text{Music}) = 14 \] 3. Calculate the probability: \[ P(\text{Music}) = \frac{14}{40} = \frac{7}{20} \] Common misconceptions: - \( \dfrac{7}{13} \) computes the odds in favor (ratio of students in Music to students not in Music, \( \frac{14}{26} \)) rather than probability. - \( \dfrac{13}{20} \) represents the complement probability (the probability that the student is NOT enrolled in Music, \( 1 - \frac{7}{20} = \frac{13}{20} \)). - \( \dfrac{7}{50} \) incorrectly assumes the total is 100 students. Final Answer: \( \dfrac{7}{20} \).

question.en: The ACT Subject Test in Mathematics consists of 50 questions in 60 minutes. If a student spends an average of 55 seconds on each of the first 30 questions, how many seconds per question are available for the remaining 20 questions?

solution.en: \(\text{Time spent on first 30 questions} = 30 \times 55 = 1650\text{ seconds}\) (27.5 minutes). \(\text{Total time available} = 60 \times 60 = 3600\text{ seconds}\). \(\text{Remaining time} = 3600 - 1650 = 1950\text{ seconds}\). For the final 20 questions: \(\frac{1950}{20} = 97.5\text{ seconds per question}\).

question.en: [Practice 3 · Medium] The graph of the quadratic function \( f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 5 \) is shown in the standard \( (x, y) \) coordinate plane below. A horizontal line \( y = k \) intersects the graph of \( f(x) \) at two points that are \( 8 \) units apart. What is the value of \( k \)?

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in Test format & strategy and start from \( f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 5 \).
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \( f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 5 \).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

solution.en: We are given the quadratic function \( f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 5 \) and a horizontal line \( y = k \) that intersects the parabola at two points separated by a horizontal distance of \( 8 \). **Method 1: Using the axis of symmetry** The axis of symmetry for a parabola in standard form \( y = ax^2 + bx + c \) is given by: \[ x = -\frac{b}{2a} = -\frac{-6}{2(1)} = 3 \] Because parabolas are symmetric about their axis of symmetry, the two intersection points on the horizontal line \( y = k \) must lie equidistant from \( x = 3 \). Since the total distance between them is \( 8 \), each point lies \( \frac{8}{2} = 4 \) units away from the line of symmetry: \[ x_1 = 3 - 4 = -1 \] \[ x_2 = 3 + 4 = 7 \] Since both points lie on the graph of \( f(x) \), the value of \( k \) is found by evaluating \( f(x) \) at either \( x = -1 \) or \( x = 7 \): \[ k = f(7) = (7)^2 - 6(7) + 5 = 49 - 42 + 5 = 12 \] \[ k = f(-1) = (-1)^2 - 6(-1) + 5 = 1 + 6 + 5 = 12 \] **Method 2: Using the quadratic formula** Setting \( f(x) = k \) gives the quadratic equation \( x^2 - 6x + (5 - k) = 0 \). Using the quadratic formula, the solutions are: \[ x = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{(-6)^2 - 4(1)(5 - k)}}{2} = 3 \pm \sqrt{9 - (5 - k)} = 3 \pm \sqrt{4 + k} \] The distance between these two roots is the difference: \[ (3 + \sqrt{4 + k}) - (3 - \sqrt{4 + k}) = 2\sqrt{4 + k} \] Setting this distance equal to \( 8 \): \[ 2\sqrt{4 + k} = 8 \implies \sqrt{4 + k} = 4 \implies 4 + k = 16 \implies k = 12 \] Common misconceptions: - Choosing \( 8 \) confuses the horizontal distance between the points with the vertical position \( k \). - Choosing \( 4 \) results from solving \( \sqrt{4 + k} = 4 \) by incorrectly writing \( 4 + k = 8 \) instead of squaring \( 4 \). - Choosing \( -3 \) results from substituting the half-distance \( x = 4 \) directly into \( f(x) \) instead of shifting from the axis of symmetry \( x = 3 \). Answer: \( 12 \).

question.en: [Practice 4 · Medium] In the standard \((x, y)\) coordinate plane, line \(L\) is perpendicular to the line \(3x + 4y = 15\) and passes through the point \((3, 1)\). Line \(L\) intersects the line \(2x + y = 17\) at the point \((p, q)\). What is the value of \(p + q\)?

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in Test format & strategy and start from \((x, y)\).
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \(3x + 4y = 15\).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

solution.en:
Step 1: Find the slope of the given line \(3x + 4y = 15\).
Rewriting in slope-intercept form gives:
\[ 4y = -3x + 15 \implies y = -\frac{3}{4}x + \frac{15}{4} \]
Thus, the slope of this line is \(m_1 = -\frac{3}{4}\).

Step 2: Determine the slope of line \(L\).
Since line \(L\) is perpendicular to the given line, its slope \(m_L\) is the negative reciprocal of \(m_1\):
\[ m_L = -\frac{1}{-\frac{3}{4}} = \frac{4}{3} \]

Step 3: Write the equation of line \(L\).
Line \(L\) passes through \((3, 1)\) with slope \(\frac{4}{3}\):
\[ y - 1 = \frac{4}{3}(x - 3) \implies y = \frac{4}{3}x - 3 \]

Step 4: Find the point of intersection \((p, q)\) with the line \(2x + y = 17\).
Substitute \(y = \frac{4}{3}x - 3\) into \(2x + y = 17\):
\[ 2x + \left(\frac{4}{3}x - 3\right) = 17 \]
\[ \frac{10}{3}x - 3 = 17 \implies \frac{10}{3}x = 20 \implies x = 6 \]
Thus, \(p = 6\).

Step 5: Solve for \(q\).
Substitute \(p = 6\) into \(2x + y = 17\):
\[ 2(6) + q = 17 \implies 12 + q = 17 \implies q = 5 \]

Step 6: Compute \(p + q\).
\[ p + q = 6 + 5 = 11 \]

Common Misconceptions:
- Reporting only \(p = 6\) or \(q = 5\) fails to answer the question, which asks for \(p + q\).
- Using the parallel slope \(-\frac{3}{4}\) instead of the perpendicular slope \(\frac{4}{3}\) yields \(p = 11\) and \(q = -5\), giving \(p + q = 6\).

question.en: [Practice 5 · Medium] The quadratic function \( f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c \) is graphed in the standard \((x, y)\) coordinate plane below. The vertex of the parabola is at \((3, -6)\), and the graph passes through the point \((1, 2)\). What is the value of \( b \)?

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in Test format & strategy and start from \( f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c \).
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \( f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k \).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

solution.en: 1. Write the quadratic function in vertex form: \( f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k \). 2. Given the vertex \((h, k) = (3, -6)\), the function is \( f(x) = a(x - 3)^2 - 6 \). 3. Use the given point \((1, 2)\) on the graph to find \( a \): \[ 2 = a(1 - 3)^2 - 6 \] \[ 2 = 4a - 6 \implies 4a = 8 \implies a = 2. \] 4. Expand the equation to standard form \( ax^2 + bx + c \): \[ f(x) = 2(x^2 - 6x + 9) - 6 = 2x^2 - 12x + 18 - 6 = 2x^2 - 12x + 12. \] 5. Comparing coefficients gives \( b = -12 \). Common error: A student who ignores the scale factor \( a \) might calculate \( b = -2h = -6 \), incorrectly choosing \(-6\). Answer: \(-12\).
